summary: Open-source AI is a structural tailwind for legacy software companies — PE bid for Workday signals software has bottomed
summary_extended: Baker argues that the proliferation of open-source AI models is structurally beneficial for legacy enterprise software companies, because a world dominated by 1-3 closed frontier model providers would create dangerous dependency risk and margin compression for software vendors, whereas open-source alternatives give software companies negotiating leverage and model optionality. He contrasts this with the bearish scenario where a handful of frontier labs extract most of the value from the software stack, suggesting open-source disrupts that dynamic in software's favor. As a real-time signal that the market may have overcorrected on software valuations, Baker points to Silver Lake's reported interest in acquiring Workday as evidence that sophisticated PE buyers see enterprise software as oversold. The investment implication is that enterprise software names — with Workday as the clearest named example — may represent a buying opportunity, and that the open-source AI trend should be monitored as a structural tailwind for the sector rather than a headwind. No specific price targets or timeframes were cited, though the PE bid dynamic suggests a near-to-medium-term catalyst for re-rating.
detail: Baker argues a world with 1-3 dominant frontier model providers is bad for software, but open-source proliferation is a 'godsend' for the American software industry. Silver Lake's potential Workday bid signals PE sees software as oversold. Open-source reduces model dependency risk for software companies.
